Sexual dimorphism in body mass is well documented among hermit hummingbirds and trochilines more broadly, and the Amethyst-throated sunangel Heliangelus amethysticollis offers a representative case within this pattern. Newly hatched nestlings emerge at a strikingly small mass of 0.53 grams [Wwb = 0.53 grams], a value consistent with the extreme altriciality typical of trochiline chicks, whose rapid early development depends heavily on intensive maternal provisioning rather than substantial endogenous reserves at hatching. As individuals approach asymptotic size, females attain a maximum recorded body mass of 5.04 grams [Wwi = 5.04 grams], while males reach a somewhat larger adult body mass of 5.8 grams [Wwi = 5.8 grams], a modest but consistent dimorphism that has been linked in related Heliangelus species to differential energetic demands associated with territorial defense and courtship display in males. This mass differential, though small in absolute terms, represents a proportionally meaningful divergence given the diminutive overall body size characteristic of high-Andean hummingbirds, and it parallels patterns reported across several congeneric sunangels inhabiting similar montane cloud-forest habitats. 

Incubation conditions strongly influence the pace of embryonic development in this species. Eggs maintained under field-relevant thermal conditions of 30 °C [T = 30 °C] hatch after approximately 17 days [ab = approximately 17 days], a duration broadly comparable to incubation periods reported for other small-bodied trochilines breeding at similar elevations. Independent of incubation temperature, resting physiological performance in post-hatching individuals has been characterized through respirometry trials conducted at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], under which conditions basal oxygen consumption reaches 27.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 27.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a comparatively high mass-specific metabolic rate that is broadly consistent with the elevated thermoregulatory costs documented across hummingbirds occupying cool montane environments. The juxtaposition of a relatively brief incubation period with a markedly elevated resting metabolic rate is suggestive of a life-history strategy favoring rapid early development at the expense of substantial daily energetic expenditure, a trade-off frequently invoked to explain the unusually fast pace of avian life histories among small nectarivorous birds. 

Reproductive output in Amethyst-throated sunangel populations appears constrained to a single annual breeding attempt under the thermal regime examined in captive and field-adjacent studies (38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]). Females typically produce 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch], with breeding limited to 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = 1 clutch per year], a low annual reproductive output that is broadly characteristic of high-elevation hummingbirds whose breeding windows are constrained by short favorable seasons and limited nectar resource availability at altitude. This conservative reproductive strategy contrasts with the comparatively higher annual fecundity reported for some lowland trochilines, where extended breeding seasons permit multiple clutches per year, and likely reflects the energetic and phenological constraints imposed by montane cloud-forest conditions. Such limited reproductive frequency is often compensated, in species exhibiting this pattern, by extended adult survival and repeated breeding opportunities across multiple seasons rather than by high per-season output, a trade-off consistent with broader life-history theory applied to small endothermic vertebrates inhabiting thermally demanding environments. 

Developmental milestones following hatching unfold over a relatively compressed timeframe under the metabolic conditions characteristic of active growth phases in this species (38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]). Nestlings achieve fledging, marked by departure from the nest and the onset of sustained independent flight, at 22 days after hatching [tx = 22 days after hatching], a pace that is typical of small-bodied trochilines whose nestling period is shortened relative to many other passerine-sized birds at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Sexual maturation follows substantially later, with attainment of sexual maturity recorded at 66 days after hatching [tp = 66 days after hatching], reflecting the additional time required to complete somatic growth and gonadal development beyond the fledgling stage at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. First successful breeding, by contrast, is delayed considerably further, occurring at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], indicating that individuals typically do not secure a breeding opportunity until they have survived a full annual cycle, likely owing to the combined constraints of territory acquisition, seasonal resource availability, and competition with established breeding adults in montane habitats at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. 

Longevity data for Amethyst-throated sunangel point to a maximum recorded lifespan of 7.5 years [am = 7.5 years], documented under the same physiological monitoring regime conducted at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] used to characterize other aspects of this species' life history. Such longevity, while modest in absolute terms, is not unusual among small Andean hummingbirds, several of which are known to persist for multiple years despite high mass-specific metabolic demands and the energetic challenges associated with daily torpor cycles at high elevation. Oldest documented individuals of this lifespan class likely benefit from reduced predation pressure typical of dense montane forest understory and from the relative climatic stability of cloud-forest elevational bands, both of which may buffer against the acute mortality risks faced by lowland congeners. Natural mortality in this species, as in most trochilines, is thought to occur predominantly through predation, extreme weather events, or age-related decline in flight and foraging efficiency rather than through any single dominant cause, consistent with patterns of senescence documented broadly across small-bodied, high-metabolic-rate avian taxa occupying thermally variable montane environments.
